blogs.title: Before POD5: The Pre-op Heparin Trap in Post-CPB Thrombocytopenia
blogs.description: Early postoperative thrombocytopenia after cardiac surgery is usually explained by CPB-related dilution and consumption, with recovery by POD2–3 and any HIT-related second fall classically between POD5–10. This case shows why a platelet fall before POD5 shouldn’t reassure: even a small preoperative heparin exposure (radial cath with 2,000 U UFH a week earlier) can prime autoimmune HIT. The post reviews expected platelet kinetics after CPB, how to adapt the 4Ts in this population, the importance of auditing all peri-procedural heparin exposures (flushes, caths, lines), and the need to stop all heparins (including LMWH prophylaxis) and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant the moment HIT is suspected.

blogs.title: When “Indeterminate” Is the Red Flag: Reading Functional HIT Assays in aHIT
blogs.description: Autoimmune HIT breaks the classic rules: heparin-independent platelet activation and, in this case, partial resistance to FcγRIIa blockade with IV.3 in the SRA. This post dissects how to interpret strong ELISA ODs alongside SRA patterns at 0, low, and supratherapeutic heparin; why serotonin release at 0 U/mL heparin and incomplete IV.3 inhibition should heighten suspicion rather than downgrade it; and when to ask the lab for PF4-enhanced SRA/PEA or repeat testing. We cover pragmatic lab communication, how antibody profiles can evolve from heparin-independent to heparin-dependent over time, and why an “indeterminate” SRA in the right clinical context is a call to treat.

blogs.title: Argatroban, Fondaparinux, or Both? Anticoagulating Fulminant aHIT After Cardiac Surgery
blogs.description: Severe aHIT with stroke demands rapid, reversible, non-heparin anticoagulation. We walk through the rationale for starting argatroban (short half-life, hepatic clearance) in profound thrombocytopenia after a fresh ischemic stroke, then pivoting to weight-based fondaparinux when hypercoagulability persists. The post highlights using fibrinogen and D‑dimer trajectories as bedside signals of anticoagulant adequacy, the role of antithrombin supplementation for fondaparinux when AT is low, practical dosing/monitoring pearls, and transitioning to a DOAC once platelets recover.

blogs.title: IVIG for Autoimmune HIT: Dosing, Mechanism, and What to Do When It Fizzles
blogs.description: High-dose IVIG can blunt aHIT by saturating Fcγ receptors and neutralizing pathogenic antibodies, often yielding a brisk platelet rise. Not always: this patient needed a third 100 g dose and still had only a modest response. We cover when to start IVIG, typical regimens, expected timelines, and safety (thrombosis, viscosity, renal risk), plus why responses may be blunted in ‘super-activating’ aHIT. Practical next steps include repeating/upping the dose, optimizing non-heparin anticoagulation, and considering adjuncts such as plasma exchange in refractory, life-threatening cases.

blogs.title: HIT-Associated Consumptive Coagulopathy: Falling Fibrinogen, Rising D‑Dimer, and the Schistocyte Trap
blogs.description: Severe HIT can mimic DIC or TTP, but the management is completely different. This post reviews the coagulation phenotype of fulminant aHIT—progressive thrombocytopenia with falling fibrinogen, rising D‑dimer, and transient schistocytes—without the ADAMTS13 deficiency of TTP. We outline how to distinguish these entities at the bedside, why platelet transfusions generally worsen HIT unless there’s life-threatening bleeding, and how serial fibrinogen/D‑dimer trends can track treatment response.

blogs.title: Stroke on the Heparin Highway: Managing Arterial Thrombosis in HIT After Cardiac Surgery
blogs.description: Arterial events, including cortical strokes, are under-recognized in HIT and can masquerade as postoperative delirium. We discuss when to image, why thrombolytics are typically off the table after recent surgery and with severe thrombocytopenia, and how to balance immediate non-heparin anticoagulation against hemorrhagic transformation risk. The post also touches on the role and timing of mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion, neuro-monitoring while anticoagulated, and how to safely transition to long-term oral anticoagulation once platelets recover.
